lessons.title: Hello, world
body: In HolyC a string literal on its own is a statement, and it prints. There is no main function to write and no include: code typed at the prompt runs as soon as you press Enter, because in TempleOS the language and the shell are the same thing.
A program is just a list of statements, run from the top. A function defined earlier can be called by a later line.

blocks.note: The string is the whole program. \n is a newline.
Print is the function the string statement calls. %s and %d stand for a string and an integer.
A string statement can take arguments after commas.

lessons.title: Types
body: The integer types say their size: I8, I16, I32 and I64 are signed, U8, U16, U32 and U64 are unsigned, and the number is the bits. F64 is a 64-bit floating-point number, Bool is true or false, and U0 means no value, the type of a function that returns nothing. There are no int, char or float keywords.
I64 is the type to reach for by default. A character is a U8; a constant like 'A' is its code.

blocks.note: A character constant is a number.

lessons.title: Numbers wrap around
body: A fixed-size integer has no room beyond its largest value: add one and it wraps to the smallest, with no error. This is what a 64-bit machine does, and HolyC does not hide it.
The same happens to a U8 at 255 and an I64 at 9,223,372,036,854,775,807.

blocks.note: 250 + 10 is 260, which does not fit in 8 bits: 260 - 256 = 4.
The largest I64, plus one, is the smallest.
A cast to a smaller type keeps only the low bits.

lessons.title: Functions
body: A function is declared with its return type first: U0 for none. A function with no arguments can be called without parentheses, which is why a lone name like Greet; on a line runs it. Arguments can have default values, and a call can leave an argument out by keeping the comma.
Define a function before the line that calls it.

blocks.note: Both lines call the same function.
Volume(, , 10) skips the first two arguments and uses their defaults.

lessons.title: Loops and choices
body: The control statements are the ones from C: if and else, for, while, do while, switch with case and default, break and continue. A switch falls through from one case to the next unless you break.

blocks.note: Case 1 has no break, so it falls through into case 2.

lessons.title: Strings and arrays
body: A string is a pointer to characters, written U8 *. Indexing gives the character code, and StrLen counts. A fixed array is declared with its size and can be filled in braces.

blocks.code:
U8 *s = "TempleOS";
"%d letters, first %c, last %c\n", StrLen(s), s[0], s[StrLen(s) - 1];

lessons.title: Classes
body: A class groups named fields, like a C struct, and a variable of that class holds all of them. Fields are reached with a dot.

blocks.note: The squared distance of (3, 4) from the origin.

lessons.title: A longer example
body: Small functions combine into programs. This one lists the prime numbers up to 50 by trial division, and then the first fifteen Fibonacci numbers.
